mse-01.title: Four Classes of Materials
explain: **Materials** are substances used to make objects. **Materials science and engineering** asks what structure a material has, what properties that structure gives it, and how it is made and processed. Spoons, window glass, plastic bags, and building columns all differ in use depending on what material they are made of.
Materials are usually divided into four classes. This classification is based on how the atoms that make up a material are bonded to one another.

- **Metals**: materials made of metallic elements such as iron, copper, and aluminum. Freely moving electrons let them conduct electricity and heat well and give them a lustrous shine. They usually stretch or bend a lot under force.
- **Ceramics**: materials made of compounds of metallic and nonmetallic elements. Pottery, bricks, cement, and glass are typical. They are usually hard and heat-resistant, do not conduct electricity well, and break easily under impact.
- **Polymers**: materials made of very long chain-shaped molecules. Plastics, rubber, and synthetic fibers are typical. They are light and easy to shape but relatively weak against heat.
- **Composite materials**: materials made by combining two or more different materials to gain the advantages of each together. Reinforced concrete, which combines cement with gravel and steel rebar, is an example.

explain.alt: A 2×2 grid lists the four classes. The metal box says 'conducts electricity and heat well' and 'usually stretches'. The ceramic box says 'hard and heat-resistant' and 'usually breaks easily'. The polymer box says 'light and easy to process' and 'relatively weak against heat'. The composite box says 'mixes two or more materials' and 'gains the advantages of each'.

explain: The traits above are **tendencies**, not laws. For example, some polymers resist heat well, and some ceramics stretch considerably. Think of the classification as a map for initially placing a material, not as a final verdict.

mse-02.title: Atomic Arrangement: Crystalline and Amorphous
explain: Materials made of the same element can differ greatly in properties depending on **how their atoms are arranged**. The arrangement is broadly divided into two types.

- **Crystal**: atoms are arranged in a regular pattern that repeats up-down and left-right. Salt grains, quartz, and most metals are like this.
- **Amorphous**: nearby atoms are connected to their neighbors, but there is no regular order extending over long distances. Glass is the typical example. A liquid that solidifies without time to form a crystal easily becomes amorphous.

explain.alt: Two panels side by side. Panel A on the left shows identical green circles arranged in a regular grid of rows and columns, labeled 'atoms line up'. Panel B on the right shows orange circles scattered with no order, labeled 'atoms are random'.
explain.caption: A is a crystal and B is an amorphous structure, drawn in simplified form.

explain: The smallest repeating unit of a crystal is called a **unit cell**. Stacking unit cells builds up the whole crystal.

A metal lump we handle is usually not one big crystal but a collection of many small crystals. Each small crystal is a **grain**, and the boundary where grains meet is a **grain boundary**. The size of the grains affects the properties of the material.

mse-03.title: Reading Properties: The Stress-Strain Curve
explain: When we talk about the properties of materials, we tend to mix up the words 'strong,' 'hard,' and 'tough.' In materials science, these words refer to different properties. The representative way to measure them is the **tensile test**. The ends of a rod-shaped specimen are gripped and slowly pulled while the force and the elongation are recorded.

To compare specimens regardless of their size, the force and the length are converted into two quantities.
- **Stress** = force ÷ cross-sectional area. Its unit is N/mm², which is called MPa.
- **Strain** = elongation ÷ original length. It is usually written as a percentage.

explain.alt: Graph with the horizontal axis showing strain (%) marked 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, and the vertical axis showing stress (MPa) marked 0, 100, 200, 300, 400, 500. The curve rises steeply and straight from the origin, bends at point P ('P: yield') and rises more gently, reaches its highest point at Q ('Q: maximum stress'), dips slightly, and ends at point R ('R: fracture').
explain.caption: Stress-strain curve of a hypothetical metal specimen

explain:
The following can be read from the curve.
- **Elastic region**: the initial straight-rising part. When the force is removed, the specimen returns to its original length. The steeper this straight line, the greater the **stiffness** (resistance to stretching).
- **Yield** (P): the point where permanent deformation begins to remain after the force is removed. Beyond this point is **plastic deformation**.
- **Tensile strength** (Q): the highest stress on the curve, the maximum stress the material withstands. **Strength** usually refers to this value or to the yield stress.
- **Fracture** (R): the point where the specimen breaks. The amount of stretching up to this point is the **ductility**.
- **Toughness**: the energy absorbed up to fracture, corresponding to the area under the curve.

**Hardness** is not measured by a tensile test but by pressing or scratching the surface, and it indicates how well the surface resists being dented or scratched. Strength, hardness, ductility, and toughness are different properties, so one being high does not mean the others are high.

mse-04.title: Metals and Alloys
explain: A metal consists of atoms stacked in layers, with electrons moving freely between them that hold the neighboring atoms together. Because of this structure, metals can be hammered thin (malleability) and drawn out (ductility). This works because the atomic layers can **slide past each other** when a force is applied.

Pure metals slide easily, so they are generally soft. That is why pure copper or aluminum can be bent fairly easily by hand. For this reason we use **alloys**, which are metals mixed with other elements.

explain.alt: Two panels. The left panel, 'Pure metal', shows several neat layers of same-sized atoms stacked on top of each other, with a 'push' label and a right-pointing arrow above the top layer, labeled 'layers slide easily'. The right panel, 'Alloy', shows the same arrangement with three larger orange atoms mixed in the middle, with the same 'push' arrow, labeled 'large atoms block sliding'.
explain.caption: In an alloy, atoms of different sizes hinder the sliding of the layers.

explain:
The reasons for making alloys depend on the application.
- To increase strength. When atoms of different sizes are mixed in, the layers become harder to slide.
- To make the metal resistant to rust and corrosion.
- To change the melting point or make it easier to process.

Representative alloys are as follows. **Steel** is iron with a small amount of carbon added. **Brass** is copper and zinc, and **bronze** is copper and tin. **Stainless steel** is iron with chromium and other elements added so that it does not rust easily.
Increasing strength generally tends to reduce ductility. Therefore, rather than maximizing a single property, the needed properties are adjusted by trading them off against one another.

mse-05.title: Polymers and Ceramics
explain: A **polymer** is a material made of long chain molecules formed by many small molecules called **monomers** linked together. The reaction that links monomers together is called **polymerization**. Properties depend on the length of the chains and on how the chains relate to one another.

explain.alt: Two panels. The left panel, 'Thermoplastic', shows four wavy chains lying side by side, separated from one another, labeled 'chains are not tied together'. The right panel, 'Thermoset', shows the same four chains connected by short orange lines (with dots at both ends) between them, labeled 'chains are linked by crosslinks'.
explain.caption: Chain structures of thermoplastics and thermosets

explain:
- **Thermoplastic** polymers: the chains are not tied to one another. Heating softens them as the chains slide past each other, and cooling makes them solid again. They can be reheated and reshaped, which makes them suited to recycling. Polyethylene and PET are examples.
- **Thermoset** polymers: the chains are linked in a net structure by **crosslinks**, a type of chemical bond. Once hardened, they do not melt and flow even when heated again; at high temperatures they char or decompose. Epoxy resin is an example.

**Ceramics** are often made of strong bonds, such as ionic or covalent bonds. Therefore, many have high melting points, are hard, and do not conduct electricity well. However, unlike metals, their atomic layers cannot easily slip, so they cannot disperse force through deformation. If a small crack is present, force concentrates at its tip, the crack spreads, and the material breaks suddenly. This property is called **brittleness**.
Glass is a typical amorphous ceramic, while pottery and bricks are ceramics made of many crystal grains.

mse-06.title: Material Selection: Comparing Properties
explain: Choosing a material is not about 'finding the strongest one.' It means listing the required conditions, comparing the candidates' properties, and weighing the properties that must be traded off against one another. This lesson only teaches how to compare, using **hypothetical practice values**. These values cannot be used for actual design or safety decisions.

When weight matters, we look not only at strength but at **specific strength**, that is, strength ÷ density. A higher specific strength generally means the material can withstand a larger force at the same weight. Cost is also considered: the mass of a part is volume × density, and the material cost is mass × unit price.

The four hypothetical candidate materials are as follows.
- Material A: density 8.0 g/cm³, strength 400 MPa, unit price 3 won/g
- Material B: density 2.7 g/cm³, strength 270 MPa, unit price 12 won/g
- Material C: density 1.2 g/cm³, strength 66 MPa, unit price 2 won/g
- Material D: density 4.5 g/cm³, strength 900 MPa, unit price 40 won/g

explain.alt: Horizontal bar chart titled 'Strength (hypothetical values, MPa)'. The bar ends are labeled 400 for material A, 270 for B, 66 for C, and 900 for D. The bar for D is the longest and the bar for C is the shortest.
explain.caption: Strength comparison of four hypothetical materials

explain: Looking at strength alone, D is the best, but its unit price is also the highest. When one property is good, other properties often get worse. This is called a **trade-off**. Ductility, toughness, workability, and corrosion resistance must also be considered.

mse-07.title: Unit Cells, Packing Fraction, and Crystal Planes
explain: In stage 1, we distinguished between crystals, whose atoms are regularly arranged, and amorphous materials, whose atoms are irregular. Properties of metals, such as why copper stretches so well and why some metals break easily, begin with the **shape** in which the atoms are stacked. This lesson learns the language for describing crystal structure quantitatively.

A crystal is built by repeating a small box of identical shape, the **unit cell**, in three dimensions. Three common structures in metals are: **simple cubic** (SC, atoms only at the corners); **body-centered cubic** (BCC, corners plus one at the center; iron and chromium at room temperature); and **face-centered cubic** (FCC, corners plus the centers of the six faces; copper, aluminum, and gold). The number of atoms that actually belong to one unit cell is counted as follows: each corner atom is shared by eight unit cells, so it contributes 1/8. Thus SC has 1 atom, BCC has 2, and FCC has 4.

The **atomic packing factor** (APF) is the fraction of a unit cell's volume occupied by atoms (spheres). Treating atoms as rigid spheres, we find the relation between the lattice parameter $a$ and the atomic radius $R$ along the direction in which the atoms touch. In FCC, atoms touch along the face diagonal, so $4R = \sqrt{2}a$, and $$APF_{FCC} = \frac{4 \times \frac{4}{3}\pi R^3}{a^3} \approx 0.74$$ 이다. BCC는 몸 대각선 방향으로 닿아 $4R = sqrt{3}a$ (in BCC, atoms touch along the body diagonal), so APF ≈ 0.68. The value 0.74 is the maximum density at which equal-sized spheres can be stacked (hexagonal close-packed, HCP, also achieves this).

Directions and planes within a crystal are expressed by **Miller indices**. They are the reciprocals of the intercepts where a plane meets the three axes, converted into integers. For cubic crystals, (100) is a plane perpendicular to one axis, (110) is a plane that cuts two axes at equal distances, and (111) is a plane that cuts all three axes at equal distances. In FCC, the (111) plane is the **close-packed plane**, where atoms are most densely arranged. As shown in the next lesson, the planes along which metals slip are usually close-packed planes.

Limitations: the rigid-sphere model simplifies atoms into spheres with sharp boundaries. In reality, bonding involves overlapping electron clouds. Also, real metals are not single crystals but polycrystals made of many small crystals with different orientations (**grains**), and the boundaries between grains strongly affect properties (lesson 3).

Step 2: $a = 4R/\sqrt{2} = 2\sqrt{2}R$, $a^3 = 16\sqrt{2}R^3 \approx 22.6R^3$. Atomic volume $4 \times 4.19R^3 = 16.8R^3$. APF $\approx 16.8/22.6 \approx 0.74$.

mse-08.title: Crystal Defects and Dislocation Slip
explain: If a crystal were perfect, an entire plane of atoms would have to slide at once for a metal to deform. The theoretical strength obtained from this calculation is hundreds to thousands of times larger than the actual strength of metals. The reason real metals deform much more easily is the **defects** in the crystal, especially **dislocations**. Defects are the 'imperfections' of a material, but materials engineers precisely control these defects to create the properties they want.

Defects are classified by dimension. **Point defects**: a vacant atomic site, a **vacancy**; an extra atom squeezed into a gap between atoms, an **interstitial atom**; and an atom that takes the place of another atom in a lattice site, a **substitutional atom**. Vacancies increase as temperature rises and assist atomic diffusion. **Line defects**: **dislocations**. **Planar defects**: grain boundaries, twin boundaries, and surfaces.

A **dislocation** is a line along which one atomic plane is inserted or displaced within a crystal. The end of the half-plane inserted in the shape of a knife edge is an **edge dislocation**. With a dislocation, the metal does not need to push a whole atomic plane at once; instead, the bonds near the dislocation line change one after another, passing the slip along. This is like moving a heavy carpet by making a fold and pushing the fold along instead of dragging the whole carpet at once. The movement of dislocations is **slip**, that is, plastic deformation of metals.

Slip does not occur in any direction. It occurs on the **close-packed plane**, where atoms are densest, and along the **close-packed direction**. The combination of plane and direction is called a **slip system**. FCC metals have many slip systems, 12 in all, so they can slip easily under forces from any direction, giving them good **ductility** (copper, aluminum, gold). HCP metals have few usable slip systems at room temperature, so they are relatively brittle (magnesium).

Key insight: **to strengthen a metal, block the movement of dislocations.** All the strengthening mechanisms of the next lesson use this principle. Limitations: dislocation theory explains the deformation of metals (crystalline materials). Ceramics barely move dislocations because of the directionality and charge of their ionic bonds, so they break without plastic deformation, while amorphous materials (glass) are not crystals and have no concept of dislocations.

examples.title: The Carpet Analogy
body: Condition: a heavy carpet is to be moved to one side of a room.
Step 1: pulling the whole carpet at once requires overcoming the friction between the entire carpet and the floor, which is very hard (the theoretical strength of a perfect crystal).

Step 2: making a fold at one end and pushing the fold along lets only the folded part move, so the carpet can be moved with little force. The fold is the dislocation, and the carpet shifting one position after the fold passes is the slip.

Interpretation: copper, with its 12 slip systems, does not crack even when bent greatly. Magnesium has few active slip systems at room temperature, so cracks easily form before large deformation. mse-09.title: Strengthening Mechanisms: Ways to Block Dislocations
explain: The conclusion of the previous lesson was that blocking the movement of dislocations strengthens a metal. Metallurgy has used this principle empirically for thousands of years. A blacksmith hammering iron and the addition of tin to bronze are both ways to block dislocations. This lesson covers four representative strengthening mechanisms.

① **Solid-solution strengthening**: when another element is dissolved into the metal (an alloy), atoms of different size distort the surrounding lattice and hinder the movement of dislocations. Brass (copper with zinc) and steel (iron with carbon) are examples. ② **Work hardening** (strain hardening): when a metal is deformed at room temperature, dislocations multiply and become tangled, blocking the motion of the next dislocations. This is why iron wire becomes harder with repeated bending until it breaks. Strength rises, but ductility falls.

③ **Grain refinement**: at grain boundaries the crystal orientation changes, making it difficult for dislocations to cross. The smaller the grains, the more boundaries there are, and the stronger the material. This relationship is the **Hall–Petch equation**. $$\sigma_y = \sigma_0 + k d^{-1/2}$$ $d$ is the average grain diameter. Grain refinement is a rare strengthening method that raises **toughness as well as strength**, so it is especially important.

explain.alt: Hall–Petch graph. Horizontal axis 1/√d (d is grain diameter, μm); vertical axis yield strength (MPa). A straight line starts at 70 MPa at 1/√d = 0 and rises to the upper right. Points are plotted at d = 100 μm (1/√d = 0.1) at 130 MPa, at d = 25 μm (0.2) at 190 MPa, and at d = 4 μm (0.5) at 370 MPa.

explain: ④ **Precipitation strengthening**: when an alloy is heated to dissolve an element, rapidly cooled, and then held at a suitable temperature (aging), very fine particles precipitate evenly throughout. These particles block the paths of dislocations. Aluminum alloys for aircraft (duralumin) are a typical example. If aging is continued too long, the particles grow coarse and sparse, and the alloy becomes weaker. This is called **overaging**.

Limitations and trade-offs: most strengthening sacrifices **ductility and toughness**. Also, a strengthened state may not hold at high temperature. Heating a work-hardened metal creates new grains and softens it again (**recrystallization**), and precipitates dissolve or coarsen at high temperature. Therefore, for high-temperature parts, one must choose strengthening mechanisms that remain stable at high temperature.

body: Condition: the line in the figure, $\sigma_0 = 70$ MPa, slope $k = 600$ MPa·μm$^{1/2}$.
Step 1: if the grain diameter is 16 μm, $d^{-1/2} = 0.25$, so $\sigma_y = 70 + 150 = 220$ MPa.

Step 2: reducing the grain size from 100 μm to 4 μm raises the yield strength from 130 to 370 MPa, about 2.8 times. This is strengthening obtained through heat treatment and processing, without changing the alloying elements.

mse-10.title: Binary Phase Diagrams and the Lever Rule
explain: The microstructure of an alloy changes with its composition and temperature. If an alloy of a specific composition is held at a specific temperature, which phases are present, and in what proportions? The map that answers this question is the **phase diagram**. Materials engineers read phase diagrams to determine heat treatment conditions.

A **phase** is a region with uniform chemical composition and structure (a liquid, or a solid with a particular crystal structure). A binary phase diagram places composition on the horizontal axis and temperature on the vertical axis, and shows as regions which phases exist under equilibrium. The simplest case is the **complete solid solubility** diagram, in which two elements mix in any ratio even in the solid state (copper–nickel).

explain.alt: Phase diagram of two metals, A and B, with complete solid solubility. Horizontal axis: mass % of B (0 to 100); vertical axis: temperature (1000 to 1500 °C). The upper liquidus line and the lower solidus line form a lens shape: above is liquid (L), below is solid (α), and inside the lens is L + α. A horizontal line at 1300 °C meets the solidus at 25% and the liquidus at 55%, and point P is marked at 35%.

explain: In the figure, the region above the **liquidus** line is entirely liquid, and the region below the **solidus** line is entirely solid (α). Inside the lens between them, liquid and solid coexist. At a point in this two-phase region, the **composition** of each phase is read where the horizontal line (**tie line**) at that temperature meets the boundary. At point P (35% B, 1300 °C), the composition of solid α is 25% B and that of the liquid is 55% B. The whole alloy is 35%, but the two phases have different compositions.

The **amount** of each phase is found with the **lever rule**. Treat the tie line as a lever with the overall composition $C_0$ as the fulcrum; the fraction of each phase is proportional to the length of the arm on the **opposite** side. $$f_L = \frac{C_0 - C_\alpha}{C_L - C_\alpha}, \quad f_\alpha = \frac{C_L - C_0}{C_L - C_\alpha}$$ 점 P에서 $f_L = (35 - 25)/(55 - 25) = 1/3$, $f_alpha = 2/3$ (at point P). This follows directly from conservation of mass.

Following the cooling process: when a 35% alloy is slowly cooled from the liquid, solid begins to form at the liquidus line (the first solid contains less B). Inside the lens, the fraction of solid steadily increases while the compositions of both phases keep changing, and at the solidus everything becomes solid. Limitation: the phase diagram assumes **equilibrium** (very slow cooling). In practice, when cooling is rapid, atoms do not have time to diffuse, so **segregation** arises, in which the composition differs between the inside and the outside of a grain. The effect of non-equilibrium is discussed with the TTT curve in lesson 3.

Step 1 (phases and compositions): liquid (55% B) + α (25% B).

Step 2 (amounts): $f_L = 1/3$, $f_\alpha = 2/3$. For a 30 g alloy, there are 10 g of liquid (containing 5.5 g of B) and 20 g of solid (containing 5 g of B). The total B is 10.5 g, which is 35% of 30 g, confirming conservation of mass.

mse-11.title: Eutectic and Eutectoid Reactions and the Iron–Carbon System
explain: Not all alloys mix in every ratio as in the previous lesson. Two elements that barely dissolve in each other in the solid state undergo unique reactions at particular compositions. The key to understanding steel, the most widely used metallic material, is the **iron–carbon phase diagram**.

**Eutectic reaction**: a liquid of a particular composition (the eutectic composition) solidifies, changing at a single temperature into **two solids simultaneously**. $L \to \alpha + \beta$. An alloy of eutectic composition has a lower melting point than the pure metals and solidifies cleanly at one temperature, which is advantageous for casting and soldering. A distinctive structure forms in which the two solids alternate in thin layers.

The **eutectoid reaction** has the same form, but instead of a liquid, **one solid** changes into two solids. $\gamma \to \alpha + \beta$. The eutectoid reaction in the iron–carbon system is the core of steel heat treatment. At about 727 °C, **austenite** (γ, FCC iron that dissolves a lot of carbon, about 0.76% carbon) transforms into a layered structure of **ferrite** (α, BCC iron that dissolves almost no carbon) and **cementite** (Fe₃C, hard and brittle), called **pearlite**.

Depending on the carbon content, **hypoeutectoid steels** (below 0.76% carbon) consist of pearlite and primary ferrite (soft), while **hypereutectoid steels** (above 0.76%) consist of pearlite and primary cementite (hard). As carbon increases, cementite increases, raising strength and hardness and reducing ductility. The proportions can be found with the lever rule. For example, when 0.4% carbon steel is cooled just below the eutectoid temperature, the pearlite fraction ≈ $(0.4 - 0.02)/(0.76 - 0.02) \approx 0.51$, and the remainder is primary ferrite.

Limitations: the Fe₃C in the iron–carbon phase diagram is strictly metastable (it can decompose into graphite if held for a very long time), and real steels contain elements such as manganese, chromium, and nickel, which shift the reaction temperatures and compositions. Also, the phase diagram is still a map for **slow cooling**. Rapid cooling produces structures not shown in the diagram (martensite), which is the subject of the next lesson.

examples.title: Structure Fractions of Hypoeutectoid Steel
body: Condition: a 0.4% carbon steel is slowly cooled to just below the eutectoid temperature. Ferrite carbon ≈ 0.02%, eutectoid composition 0.76%.
Step 1: pearlite fraction $\approx (0.4 - 0.02)/(0.76 - 0.02) = 0.38/0.74 \approx 0.51$.
Step 2: primary ferrite about 49%. For a 0.6% carbon steel, the pearlite fraction is about 0.78, and the steel is harder.

mse-12.title: TTT Curves and Heat Treatment of Steel
explain: The same steel can become hard and blade-like or soft and wire-like depending on its heat treatment. This is why a blacksmith quenches heated metal in water (quenching). The phase diagram in the previous lesson was a map for slow cooling. This lesson covers the structures produced by the **cooling rate**, and the **TTT curve** that displays them.

When austenite is **suddenly** cooled to a temperature below the eutectoid temperature and held there, the transformation to pearlite does not happen instantly but takes time, because atoms (especially carbon) must diffuse to separate into cementite and ferrite. The graph connecting the start and finish times of the transformation at each temperature is the **TTT** (time–temperature–transformation) curve. Its shape resembles the letter C.

Why the curve is C-shaped: just below the eutectoid temperature, the **driving force** for transformation is small, so it is slow; at very low temperatures, atomic **diffusion** is slow, so it is also slow. The transformation is fastest at the middle (the nose). Transformation at high temperatures yields coarse pearlite (soft), transformation near the nose yields fine pearlite (harder), and below the nose **bainite** forms.

**Martensite**: if the steel is cooled rapidly enough to avoid the nose (quenching) down to a very low temperature, carbon has no time to diffuse. The FCC austenite then changes without diffusion, its atoms shifting collectively in an instant, to form martensite, a distorted structure with carbon trapped inside. It is extremely hard but brittle. Therefore, after quenching, the steel is reheated to a suitable temperature in **tempering** (reheating), which precipitates part of the carbon as fine carbides and restores toughness. **Quenching + tempering** is the standard heat treatment for high-strength steel.

Other heat treatments: **annealing** (heating sufficiently, then cooling very slowly inside the furnace, producing softness that is easy to work), and **normalizing** (cooling in air, making the grains uniform and fine). Limitation: the TTT curve is the result of experiments that **hold at a constant temperature**. Real parts cool continuously, so the continuous cooling transformation (CCT) curve is used instead. Also, in thick parts the cooling rate differs between the surface and the center, so the microstructure and hardness vary with position. This lesson covers principles and is not a practical heat-treatment guide.

examples.title: Cooling Paths and Microstructures
body: Path 1: austenite is slowly cooled in the furnace → coarse pearlite → soft and ductile (annealing).
Path 2: rapidly quenched in water to avoid the nose → martensite → extremely hard and brittle.
Path 3: after Path 2, reheated to about 400 °C for tempering → tempered martensite → a balance of strength and toughness.

Interpretation: the surface cools quickly and becomes martensite, but the center cools more slowly, passes the nose, and becomes pearlite or bainite. The surface is hard while the center is less hard. To harden the center as well, alloying elements such as chromium and molybdenum are added to shift the nose of the TTT curve to the right (longer times), increasing the **hardenability**.

mse-13.title: Fracture Toughness and Griffith Theory
explain: A glass window breaks in an instant, starting from a small scratch. Large ships and bridges have also suddenly broken apart from small cracks. The strength of a material alone cannot predict such failures. The discipline that deals with how much a material withstands **when a crack is present** is **fracture mechanics**.

Griffith explained why the actual strength of glass is much lower than its theoretical strength by **microscopic cracks**. Stress concentrates greatly at the crack tip (the stress concentration covered in an earlier stage). The sharper and longer the crack, the greater the concentration. As a crack grows, the elastic energy stored in the material is released, but creating new surfaces requires energy. The moment the released energy exceeds the surface energy required, the crack grows rapidly on its own.

Modern fracture mechanics expresses the stress state at the crack tip with the **stress intensity factor** $K = Y\sigma\sqrt{\pi a}$. Here $\sigma$ is the applied stress, $a$ is the crack length (the depth for a surface crack or the half-length for an internal crack), and $Y$ is a geometry factor (roughly 1). When $K$ reaches the material-specific **fracture toughness** $K_{IC}$, fracture occurs. $$\sigma_f = \frac{K_{IC}}{Y\sqrt{\pi a}}$$ If the crack becomes four times longer, the stress it can withstand is halved.

Approximate sizes of fracture toughness (MPa·m$^{1/2}$): glass about 0.7, typical ceramics 3–5, aluminum alloys 20–40, and steel 50–150. Ceramics have low fracture toughness even when their strength is high, so they are very sensitive to small defects. In metals, plastic deformation occurs at the crack tip, blunting the crack and absorbing energy, which gives them high fracture toughness.

Design implications: if the smallest crack size that can be detected in a part (the inspection capability) is known, the fracture toughness determines the allowable stress. Conversely, once the operating stress is set, the dangerous crack size can be calculated, and inspection intervals are set so that cracks are found while still smaller than that (damage-tolerant design). Limitation: $K_{IC}$ is a plane-strain value for thick specimens, and some steels lose fracture toughness sharply at low temperatures (ductile-to-brittle transition). This lesson covers concepts and is not a practical guideline for judging structural safety.

body: Condition: steel plate with fracture toughness 50 MPa·m$^{1/2}$, operating stress 200 MPa, $Y = 1$.
Step 1: $a_c = \frac{1}{\pi}\left(\frac{K_{IC}}{\sigma}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{\pi}(0.25)^2 \approx 0.0199$ m.
Step 2: about 20 mm. Inspection must be able to find cracks much smaller than this to provide a safety margin.

examples.title: Comparing Ceramics and Metals

Step 2: aluminum $\approx 30/0.056 \approx 535$ MPa (yielding would occur first). Ceramics are very sensitive to small defects.

mse-14.title: Fatigue Failure and S–N Curves
explain: A paper clip does not break after being bent once, but if it is bent back and forth many times, it eventually breaks. A material can fail under **repeated** application of stress much lower than its yield strength. This is **fatigue**. Most failures of machine parts are said to originate from fatigue, so it is among the most important considerations in design.

Fatigue failure proceeds in three stages. ① **Crack initiation**: a tiny crack forms at a place where stress concentrates, such as a surface scratch, a corner, or an inclusion. ② **Crack propagation**: the crack grows slightly with each load cycle. Beach-like striations remain on the fracture surface. ③ **Final fracture**: the remaining cross-section can no longer support the load and breaks suddenly. Most of the total life is spent in initiation and propagation, and the final fracture happens in an instant.

explain.alt: S-N curve. Horizontal axis: number of cycles to failure N (10³ to 10⁸, logarithmic scale); vertical axis: stress amplitude (MPa). The solid line for steel starts at 500 MPa at 10³ cycles, declines, and becomes horizontal at about 250 MPa after 10⁶ cycles. A point at (10⁵ cycles, 333 MPa) is marked. The dashed line for an aluminum alloy keeps descending and has no horizontal section.

explain: The **S-N curve** shows the experimentally obtained relation between the stress amplitude (S) and the number of cycles to failure (N). The lower the stress, the longer the material lasts. For some iron-based alloys such as steel, the curve becomes horizontal after about $10^6$ to $10^7$ cycles; below this stress the material survives virtually indefinitely. This is called the **fatigue limit** (roughly half the tensile strength). Nonferrous metals such as aluminum alloys have no clear fatigue limit, so the **fatigue strength**, the strength at a specified number of cycles (for example, $10^7$ or $10^8$ cycles), is used instead.

Methods to extend fatigue life: polish the surface smooth (removing scratches), round the corners to reduce stress concentration, and introduce **compressive residual stress** into the surface (shot peening, in which small beads are fired at the surface to compress the surface layer). When the mean stress is tensile, life decreases; when it is compressive, life increases. In corrosive environments, the fatigue limit can disappear (corrosion fatigue). Limitation: S-N data scatter widely even under the same conditions, so designs include statistical margins. Actual loads vary in magnitude, so they are approximated with cumulative damage rules (such as Miner's rule).

Step 2: if a rotating shaft turns 1,000 times per minute and the stress is applied once per revolution, $10^5$ cycles is about 100 minutes. It would not survive even a day. The design must stay below the fatigue limit.

mse-15.title: High-Temperature Creep
explain: Old lead roofs sag over the years, and turbine blades in jet engines gradually stretch after thousands of hours of operation. Even when the stress is below the yield strength, a material keeps deforming slowly under load **for a long time at high temperature**. This is **creep**. It is the key phenomenon that determines the life of high-temperature parts in power plants, engines, and chemical plants.

Creep becomes significant at about 0.3 to 0.4 times the melting point (in kelvin) or higher. Thus lead, with a melting point of 600 K, creeps even at room temperature (300 K, 0.5 times its melting point), while iron (about 1800 K) becomes a concern only above several hundred degrees. At high temperatures, atomic **diffusion** is active, so dislocations can bypass obstacles by climbing, and grain boundaries slide.

When strain is plotted against time under constant stress and temperature, three stages appear. ① **Primary creep**: at first fast, then gradually slowing as work hardening builds up. ② **Secondary creep** (steady state): hardening and recovery balance, so the strain rate is nearly constant. This stage covers most of the life and is the basis for design. ③ **Tertiary creep**: internal cavities form and the cross-section narrows, the rate surges, and the material fractures.

The steady-state creep rate depends strongly on stress and temperature. $$\dot{\varepsilon} = A\sigma^n e^{-Q/RT}$$ $n$은 보통 3~8이고, $e^{-Q/RT}$는 화학 4단계의 아레니우스 식과 같은 형태다(활성화 에너지 $Q$). 응력을 두 배로 하면 속도가 $2^n$배(예: $n = 5$면 32배). In other words, n is usually 3 to 8, and the exponential term has the same form as the Arrhenius equation in chemistry (stage 4), with activation energy Q. Doubling the stress multiplies the rate by 2^n (for example, 32 times when n = 5), and even a small rise in temperature increases the rate greatly.

Designing for creep resistance: materials with high melting points, stable precipitates that do not dissolve at high temperature, large grains or **single crystals** that eliminate grain-boundary sliding (turbine blades are made as a single crystal), and coatings that prevent oxidation. It is interesting that grain refinement, useful for room-temperature strengthening, can be disadvantageous for high-temperature creep. Limitation: it is difficult to run creep tests lasting tens of thousands of hours in the laboratory, so results from short tests at higher temperature or stress are extrapolated, which carries uncertainty.

mse-16.title: Energy Bands and Semiconductor Doping
explain: Copper conducts electricity very well, glass hardly conducts at all, and silicon lies in between. Moreover, adding a very small amount of impurity to silicon can change its conductivity by a factor of millions. This remarkable difference is explained by the energy states of electrons in solids, the **energy band** structure. The entire modern electronics industry rests on this principle.

An electron in a single atom has discrete energy levels (Physics, stage 5). When atoms gather into a solid, the influence of neighboring atoms broadens each level into a **band**. The highest band filled with electrons is the **valence band**, the band above it is the **conduction band**, and the range of energies that electrons cannot have between them is the **band gap** ($E_g$). For current to flow, electrons must move into empty energy states where they can travel.

explain.alt: Energy band diagrams of three materials. In each panel, the bottom is the valence band and the top is the conduction band. (A) The two bands overlap. (B) The band gap is narrow, at 1.1 eV. (C) The band gap is wide, at 9 eV.

explain: The three cases in the figure: (A) **conductor**: the bands overlap or are partially filled, so electrons easily move into nearby empty states. (B) **Semiconductor**: the band gap is small (about 1.1 eV for silicon), so thermal energy at room temperature lifts some electrons into the conduction band. The electrons that have moved up, together with the empty spaces left in the valence band (**holes**), carry the current. (C) **Insulator**: the band gap is large (for example, about 9 eV), so almost no electrons are lifted at room temperature. In semiconductors, conductivity **increases** as temperature rises, whereas in metals it **decreases**, because atomic vibrations obstruct the electrons.

**Doping**: adding a very small amount of phosphorus (P), which has five valence electrons, to pure silicon (four valence electrons) leaves one extra electron that easily moves into the conduction band, giving an **n-type** semiconductor. Adding boron (B), which has three valence electrons, leaves one bond short of an electron, creating a hole, which gives a **p-type** semiconductor. Changing only about one in a million to one in a hundred million silicon atoms is enough to change the conductivity greatly. Joining p-type and n-type material creates a **pn junction** (a diode), covered in Electrical and Electronic Engineering, stage 4.

The band gap is also connected to light. Photons with energy larger than the band gap can lift electrons across the gap (solar cells, photodetectors). Conversely, when an electron falls from the conduction band to the valence band, it emits light whose energy equals the band gap; this is the principle of the LED. A band gap of 2 eV corresponds to light of about 620 nm (red) ($\lambda \approx 1240/E_g$ nm, with $E_g$ in eV). Limitation: band theory is an approximation for crystalline solids, and materials whose band gap is 'indirect,' like silicon, do not emit light efficiently, so other semiconductors are used for LEDs.

mse-17.title: Dielectric and Magnetic Materials
explain: A single smartphone contains capacitors that store electric charge, filters that separate signals, magnets in the speaker that produce sound, and magnetic recording devices that store data. Materials that do not conduct current also play important roles by responding to electric and magnetic fields. This lesson covers **dielectrics** and **magnetic materials**.

A **dielectric** does not conduct electricity, but when it is placed in an electric field, its internal charges shift slightly (**polarization**). Inserting a dielectric between the plates of a capacitor increases the charge stored at the same voltage. The capacitance is $C = \varepsilon_r\varepsilon_0\frac{A}{d}$, and it is larger when the **relative permittivity** $\varepsilon_r$ is larger. Vacuum is 1, paper is about 3, water is about 80, and ferroelectric ceramics such as barium titanate reach several thousand. This is why small multilayer ceramic capacitors can have large capacitance.

Another important property of dielectrics is the **dielectric strength**, the electric field strength a dielectric can withstand before its insulation breaks down. To make a capacitor smaller, the thickness $d$ must be reduced, but at the same voltage the field $V/d$ grows, increasing the risk of breakdown. Some crystals (quartz, piezoelectric ceramics) develop a voltage when pressed and deform when a voltage is applied, a property called **piezoelectricity**. It is used in sensors, ultrasonic devices, and clock resonators.

**Magnetic materials**: the spin and orbital motion of electrons inside atoms act as tiny magnets. **Ferromagnetic materials** such as iron, nickel, and cobalt have regions (**magnetic domains**) in which the atomic magnets of neighboring atoms align in the same direction. Applying an external magnetic field aligns the domains and strongly magnetizes the material. A material that retains much of its magnetization after the field is removed, and is hard to demagnetize, is a **hard magnetic material** (a permanent magnet). One that magnetizes and demagnetizes easily is a **soft magnetic material** (such as a transformer core).

Repeatedly magnetizing a material traces a **hysteresis loop**, whose area is proportional to the energy lost as heat in each cycle. Transformer cores reverse their magnetization tens to hundreds of times per second, so narrow-loop soft magnetic materials (silicon steel sheets) are used to reduce the loss. Permanent magnets need a wide, 'fat' loop so that they keep their magnetization despite external influences. Limitation: ferromagnetism disappears above the **Curie temperature** (about 770 °C for iron). Therefore, magnets used at high temperature must be chosen from materials with a high Curie temperature.

mse-18.title: Glass Transition of Polymers and Properties of Ceramics
explain: A plastic ruler is rigid at room temperature but bends when placed in hot water, and a rubber band becomes stiff when placed in a freezer. A ceramic bowl is very hard but breaks when dropped. This lesson covers the distinctive properties of **polymers** and **ceramics**, two material families that differ from metals, along with their causes.

**Polymers** are long-chain molecules made of thousands to tens of thousands of small units (monomers) linked together. They contain a mixture of **amorphous** regions, where chains are disordered and tangled, and **crystalline** regions, where chains are aligned side by side. The key to how properties change with temperature is the **glass transition temperature** ($T_g$). Below $T_g$, the chains cannot move, so the material is in a rigid, brittle **glassy state**. Above it, some chain segments move, and the material becomes soft and stretchable, a **rubbery state**. A rubber band has a $T_g$ tens of degrees below zero, so it is rubbery at room temperature, and when it approaches $T_g$ in the freezer, it stiffens.

Polymers behave in two groups when heated. **Thermoplastic** polymers (polyethylene, PET): the chains are held together only by weak forces, so they melt when heated and solidify when cooled, and they can be remelted and recycled. **Thermosetting** polymers (epoxy, phenolic resin): the chains are linked by chemical bonds (crosslinks) into a net, so once hardened they do not melt when heated again but char and burn. **Elastomers** (rubber), with appropriate crosslinking, can be stretched greatly and return to their original shape.

**Ceramics** are materials made of metal and nonmetal elements bonded ionically or covalently (aluminum oxide, silicon carbide, glass). **High melting points, hardness, chemical stability, and good electrical and thermal insulation** result from their strong bonds. However, they barely move dislocations (lesson 1), so they break without plastic deformation, and their low fracture toughness (stage 4) makes them very sensitive to small defects. Therefore, the strength of ceramics scatters widely and is treated statistically, using a “weakest link” model in which the largest flaw determines the strength.

Ways to compensate for ceramic weaknesses: precise powder processing that reduces flaws, tempered glass with compressive stress on its surface (which breaks into small, harmless pieces, making it safer), and composite materials with embedded fibers. The weaknesses of polymers (low stiffness and heat resistance) are compensated by **composite materials** containing glass or carbon fibers. Limitation: polymers slowly degrade under ultraviolet light and heat, and under sustained load even at room temperature they creep (the lower a polymer's $T_g$, the stronger this effect).

Step 2: rubber is above its $T_g$, so it is in the rubbery state. In boiling water (100 °C), polystyrene softens and deforms, so it is unsuitable for hot beverages.

mse-19.title: Integrated Problem Solving: Material Selection Map and Performance Index
explain: The first lesson of the capstone deals systematically with the final question of materials engineering: '**what** should this part be made of?' Choosing from tens of thousands of materials cannot be done by intuition. Required properties must be quantified, candidates must be narrowed on a material property map, and the final conditions must be set using microstructure and processing knowledge from stages 2 to 5.

**Step 1 (function and constraints)**: example: a bicycle frame tube. Function: a beam that carries bending loads. Objective: light weight (minimize mass). Constraints: a required stiffness (it must not bend too much) and strength, and a fixed length. Free variable: the cross-sectional size.

**Step 2 (performance index)**: for a light beam with a fixed stiffness, adjusting the cross-section to meet the stiffness makes the mass proportional to $\frac{\rho}{E^{1/2}}$. Therefore, $\frac{E^{1/2}}{\rho}$ should be large. This value is called the **performance index**. For a simple tensile rod, the index is $E/\rho$ (specific stiffness). The key point is that the index depends on the loading mode. On a material property map (density on the horizontal axis, elastic modulus on the vertical axis, both on logarithmic scales), materials with the same index lie on one straight line, so materials above that line are candidates.

**Step 3 (comparing candidates)**: rough values: steel ($E = 210$ GPa, $\rho = 7.8$), aluminum alloy (70, 2.7), titanium alloy (110, 4.5), carbon-fiber composite (about 100, 1.6). $E^{1/2}/\rho$: steel 1.86, aluminum 3.10, titanium 2.33, composite 6.25. For bending stiffness, the composite is the lightest, and aluminum is more favorable than steel. With the tensile index $E/\rho$, steel gives 26.9 and aluminum 25.9, which are nearly equal.

**Step 4 (microstructure and processing)**: if aluminum is chosen, an alloy strengthened by precipitation (stage 2) is used, and the heat treatment conditions (solution treatment and aging) are set. It is also necessary to consider that in welded regions, the heat can dissolve or coarsen the precipitates and weaken the area. To address fatigue (stage 4), the corners of the welds are ground smooth. If a composite is chosen, internal damage such as delamination from impact may not be visible from the outside, so inspection methods are important.

**Critique**: a performance index considers only one objective. In practice, cost, workability, fatigue, impact toughness, corrosion, and recyclability must be considered together. Carbon fiber is the lightest but is expensive and difficult to recycle. In the end, this is a multi-objective trade-off, and the index is only a starting point for narrowing the candidates.

mse-20.title: Capstone: Material and Process Design Report
explain: The final task is to **choose a hypothetical part, select a material that meets its required properties, design a process to obtain the desired microstructure, and critique those choices**. Examples: a kitchen knife blade, a smartphone back panel, a climbing carabiner, an electric vehicle battery case, or a semiconductor heat sink. This is not an actual product design or a safety certification.

Report outline: ① **Function and required properties of the part**: type of load (tension, bending, cyclic, impact), temperature, environment (corrosion, humidity), electrical and thermal requirements, and weight and cost targets. ② **Performance index and candidates**: an index matched to the loading mode, two or three candidate materials, and a numerical comparison. ③ **Final material and microstructure targets**: crystal structure, grain size, phase composition, precipitates, and so on. ④ **Process design**: the order and rationale for casting, working, heat treatment (quenching, tempering, aging), and surface treatment, based on phase-diagram and TTT evidence. ⑤ **Failure mode check**: which of yielding, fracture (toughness), fatigue, creep, and corrosion is dominant. ⑥ **Critique**: trade-offs (strength vs. toughness, weight vs. cost), uncertainties, and recycling and environmental impact.

Features of a good report: convert words like 'strong' and 'light' into numbers. Material choice and process choice are **linked** (if you chose a precipitation-hardened alloy, state its aging conditions). Find the most dangerous failure mode and design against it. Do not write only the advantages; also write the material's weaknesses and countermeasures.
This task is not graded. The report you submit is stored only on this device and can be viewed again under 'My progress' in 'Notes I left.'

examples.title: Model Outline: A Hypothetical Kitchen Knife Blade
body: Required properties: hardness at the edge (it stays sharp for a long time), sufficient toughness (the edge does not chip), and no rust.
Material: martensitic stainless steel with at least 13% chromium (chromium forms a surface oxide film that prevents corrosion, and carbon provides hardening).
Process: austenitizing → quenching (avoiding the TTT nose, producing martensite) → low-temperature tempering (keeps the hardness while partly restoring toughness).

Failure modes: micro-cracks at the edge (fracture toughness) and wear during repeated use. Critique: the harder the blade, the lower its toughness, so the edge chips more easily, and the balance is set by the tempering temperature.

Pitfall 2: assuming that finer grains are always better (they can be disadvantageous at high temperature).
Pitfall 3: choosing a material but leaving out the process (the same steel can behave completely differently depending on whether it is quenched).
